rules: Acceptable National Polygon overlaps can occur where registrations exist at different floor levels, strata, tenures or classes of title.
Caseworkers can classify an overlap as acceptable and allow it to remain in the National Polygon dataset.
HM Land Registry describes illegal overlapping polygons as overlaps that should not exist in the data.
On system referral of an index-polygon overlap, a caseworker investigates the overlap.
A caseworker may resolve an index-polygon overlap when the data can be corrected.
Where registered title extents genuinely overlap, HM Land Registry has limited powers to amend the registered extents until an application to amend or rectify is received.
National Polygon overlaps smaller than 0.5 square metres are not referred to caseworkers for remedial action.
HM Land Registry explains that overlaps below 0.5 square metres are considered insignificant and too small to resolve satisfactorily with the mapping toolset.
Adjoining registrations are considered as part of the land-registration process.
Where titles are intended to adjoin, HM Land Registry practice advises that minor index-polygon discrepancies should be resolved.
Some registered titles are legitimately not intended to adjoin, and their index polygons may therefore not adjoin.
HM Land Registry practice allows an index-polygon extent to be the same size as, larger than or smaller than the extent shown on the title plan.
National Polygon index polygons should not be relied upon to show the exact extent of registered titles.
The National Polygon dataset includes polygons based on former practices and therefore contains historical inconsistencies.
Historic index polygons were manually captured on Ordnance Survey county-series sheets.
Historic index polygons were manually captured on national-grid sheets.
Historic index polygons were manually captured in parcels books.
In February 2004 HM Land Registry completed a project converting about 19 million paper index polygons to vectorised polygons.
The 2004 vectorisation programme mapped converted polygons against Ordnance Survey Land-Line.
During mass vectorisation HM Land Registry introduced a temporary practice in which index polygons were completed pictorially.
During that temporary vectorisation practice, title plans were seldom used to validate an indexed extent.
Index polygons affected by Ordnance Survey's Positional Accuracy Programme were subsequently amended.
HM Land Registry's Positional Accuracy Improvement programme ran from 2005 to 2008.
Many polygons affected by positional-accuracy work were moved automatically in sympathy with Ordnance Survey mapping.
Polygons that did not meet automated positional-accuracy criteria were referred for manual investigation against the title plan.
Around 2009 HM Land Registry began the Quality Improvement Flowline initiative for index polygons.
Almost 14 million index polygons went through the Quality Improvement Flowline process.
The Quality Improvement Flowline resolved some minor polygon overlaps.
The Quality Improvement Flowline used automated extent matching and reconciled index polygons with title plans.
By the Quality Improvement Flowline period HM Land Registry was using OS MasterMap, which replaced OS Land-Line.
HM Land Registry receives a daily change-only update of OS MasterMap.
The daily OS MasterMap change-only update is used when creating new index polygons.
The daily OS MasterMap change-only update is used when creating new title plans.
The daily OS MasterMap change-only update is not used to routinely review or update existing registrations.
Existing index polygons are updated when there is appropriate activity on a title or when an adjoining title demands a change.
Large-scale Ordnance Survey mapping used for HM Land Registry capture can be at 1:1,250 scale in urban areas.
Large-scale Ordnance Survey mapping used for HM Land Registry capture can be at 1:2,500 scale in semi-urban and rural areas.
Large-scale Ordnance Survey mapping used for HM Land Registry capture can be at 1:10,000 scale in mountain and moorland areas.
The current-practice Indicative Extent feature type is the most common National Polygon feature type.
Footprint indexing captures an area larger than the title extent where multiple titles in one building would otherwise be difficult to interpret.
A footprint index polygon is normally captured to the smallest building footprint that fully accommodates the title extent.
Registered land outside a building footprint, such as garden ground or parking, should be represented by separate indicative-extent polygons.
Artificial Footprint indexing is used where many floor-level registrations affect an unusually large defined area.
Artificial Footprint indexing is commonly encountered in shopping malls, small-plot schemes and bin stores.
Exaggerated Extent index polygons are required to have a width of at least one metre so very narrow registered land can be identified.
Where a narrow registered strip adjoins other registered land, the adjoining index polygon can be reduced to allow the strip to be shown at one metre width.
Under the former Gridding practice, index polygons crossing national-grid sheet joins were split at the sheet joins.
Parts created by former Gridding practice can each have their own Polygon ID.
Before publication, overnight National Polygon validation checks for zero-coordinate polygons, zero-area polygons and duplicate coordinate points.
The National Polygon publication process removes zero-area polygons and polygons with an area below 0.1 square metres.
The Planning Data entity-search q parameter can search by postcode.
The Planning Data entity-search q parameter can search by Unique Property Reference Number.
Planning Data states that a UPRN query is more precise than a coordinate query for registered properties.
The Planning Data entity-search typology parameter accepts one or more typology values.
The Planning Data entity-search organisation_entity parameter accepts one or more organisation entity identifiers.
The Planning Data entity-search entity parameter accepts one or more entity numbers.
The Planning Data entity-search curie parameter accepts one or more CURIE values.
The Planning Data entity-search prefix parameter accepts one or more prefix values.
The Planning Data entity-search reference parameter accepts one or more reference values.
The Planning Data geometry_relation parameter supports the within relation.
The Planning Data geometry_relation parameter supports the equals relation.
The Planning Data geometry_relation parameter supports the disjoint relation.
The Planning Data geometry_relation parameter supports the intersects relation.
The Planning Data geometry_relation parameter supports the touches relation.
The Planning Data geometry_relation parameter supports the contains relation.
The Planning Data geometry_relation parameter supports the covers relation.
The Planning Data geometry_relation parameter supports the coveredby relation.
The Planning Data geometry_relation parameter supports the overlaps relation.
The Planning Data geometry_relation parameter supports the crosses relation.
When a WKT polygon is passed to Planning Data, spaces in the WKT must be percent-encoded.
Planning Data notes that most HTTP client libraries handle WKT space percent-encoding automatically.
The geometry_entity parameter allows a query to use the geometry of an existing Planning Data entity instead of embedding a raw polygon.
Planning Data examples use local-planning-authority entity identifiers as reusable geometry_entity boundaries for spatial queries.
Live Planning Data entity pages expose a CURIE alongside prefix and reference fields.
Live Planning Data entity pages expose an organisation-entity identifier when an organisation manages the entity.
A live Planning Data geography entity can expose a WKT point even when its geometry field is empty.
Planning Data uses the quality label authoritative for data obtained from an authoritative source.
Planning Data uses the quality label some where some data is available from an alternative source.
The Planning Data platform collects planning and housing data from local planning authorities and transforms it into a consistent state across England.
Planning Data states that its current product does not yet provide complete coverage of all England and that collected data can still be incomplete.
ArcGIS WCS connections on the Defra Data Services Platform do not support raster statistics directly.
Environment Agency guidance says WCS rasters in ArcGIS are viewed using a stretch renderer.
The published global symbology minimum for the LIDAR Composite DTM 1m is -409.05 metres; this is a dataset-wide display statistic, not a candidate elevation.
The published global symbology maximum for the LIDAR Composite DTM 1m is 978.05 metres; this is a dataset-wide display statistic, not a candidate elevation.
The published global symbology mean for the LIDAR Composite DTM 1m is 104.63 metres; this is a dataset-wide display statistic, not a candidate elevation.
The published global symbology standard deviation for the LIDAR Composite DTM 1m is 107.52 metres; this is a dataset-wide display statistic, not a candidate elevation.
Environment Agency WCS GeoTIFF responses use -3.4028235e+38 as the NoData value.
In an Environment Agency WCS GeoTIFF, NoData is encoded as a numeric pixel value in the two-dimensional raster array rather than as a text string.
How the WCS NoData value is displayed depends on the client application.
Environment Agency guidance notes that WCS layers appearing black or showing infinity values in ArcGIS can be a default-symbology issue.
Environment Agency guidance directs ArcGIS users to the Symbology pane to correct black or infinity WCS display problems.
The Dynamic Range Adjustment option can apply WCS display statistics to the current screen extent.
ArcGIS users can alternatively enter custom minimum and maximum statistics for the WCS renderer.
The ArcGIS Pro Make WCS Layer tool is available with Basic, Standard and Advanced licence levels.
For the Defra WCS connection in ArcGIS Pro, the documented URL is entered only up to the question mark after the WCS path.
ArcGIS Pro can automatically populate a template extent after the Environment Agency WCS URL is entered.
Users can change the WCS template extent before running the ArcGIS Pro Make WCS Layer tool.
ArcGIS Pro can automatically select the Input WCS Coverage after the Environment Agency WCS URL is entered.
The Environment Agency documentation demonstrates Dynamic Range Adjustment with a two-standard-deviation stretch for a local WCS view.
The LIDAR Ground Truth Surveys dataset is an archive of independently surveyed elevation points used to verify Environment Agency time-stamped LIDAR accuracy.
Environment Agency ground-truth surveys were captured by various independent surveyors.
A ground-truth survey consists of a few hundred points rather than a dense wall-to-wall raster.
Ground-truth points are captured on flat, unambiguous surfaces.
A tarmac car park is given as an example of a suitable ground-truth surface.
A tennis court is given as an example of a suitable ground-truth surface.
Ground-truth elevation points are surveyed using GPS.
Each Environment Agency ground-truth point has an accuracy of approximately plus or minus 3 centimetres RMSE.
Ground-truth point attributes include the date of survey.
Ground-truth point attributes include the surface type.
Ground-truth point attributes include the survey method.
Ground-truth point attributes include the transformation model used.
Ground-truth point attributes include the geoidal model used.
A ground-truth survey can potentially be reused for multiple LIDAR surveys when it is less than five years old.
For coastal projects, Environment Agency ground-truth reuse is limited to surveys less than three years old.
Environment Agency time-stamped LIDAR is compared with ground-truth observations to calculate RMSE.
The Environment Agency ground-truth comparison also assesses standard deviation.
The Environment Agency ground-truth comparison also assesses random error.
Environment Agency quality control requires LIDAR surveys to report an RMSE below plus or minus 15 centimetres.
The Ground Truth Surveys metadata states a 10-centimetre threshold for standard deviation and random error in quality control.
The LIDAR Ground Truth Surveys dataset is available as a file geodatabase download.
The LIDAR Ground Truth Surveys dataset is available as a GeoJSON download.
The LIDAR Ground Truth Surveys dataset is available as a GeoPackage download.
The LIDAR Ground Truth Surveys dataset is available as an ESRI Shapefile download.
The LIDAR Ground Truth Surveys metadata exposes an OGC API Features service.
The Defra open-data portal limits ordinary LIDAR download selection to 5 kilometre by 5 kilometre tiles.
The portal can download several LIDAR tiles at once, but only for relatively small areas.
The ordinary online portal does not provide a bulk download for the whole country or a very large area.
Very large Environment Agency LIDAR supplies are handled through an offline large-data supply process rather than the ordinary tile portal.
For a 50-centimetre Environment Agency surface model, the average source point-cloud density is at least 4 points per square metre.
For a 25-centimetre Environment Agency surface model, the average source point-cloud density is at least 16 points per square metre.
Environment Agency point-density figures are defined for the DSM made from the last or only laser return, not for the DTM.
Under vegetation, DTM point density does not necessarily reach the nominal density associated with the output resolution.
Point density can increase where multiple LIDAR flight lines overlap.
Point density can vary in the forward-scan direction where terrain changes significantly.
Environment Agency point clouds are irregular collections of points, so the agency describes their density rather than calling the point cloud itself a regular-grid resolution.
OS Terrain 50 GeoPackage delivery uses a single national file that is straightforward to transfer.
Ordnance Survey describes the single GeoPackage as providing a richer end-user experience than many-file delivery.
GeoPackage attribute names are not limited in length, allowing more user-friendly OS Terrain 50 field names.
The documented GeoPackage format has a theoretical file-size limit of 140 TB.
The effective GeoPackage file-size limit can be lower where the destination file system imposes its own limit.
GeoPackage supports raster content.
GeoPackage supports vector content.
GeoPackage supports database-style content.
In OS Terrain 50 GeoPackage naming, the 2022 attribute Fid became fid in the 2023 naming scheme.
In OS Terrain 50 GeoPackage naming, the 2022 attribute Id became id in the 2023 naming scheme.
In OS Terrain 50 GeoPackage naming, propertyValue became property_value.
The separate propertyValue_uom attribute is not present in the newer OS Terrain 50 GeoPackage naming table.
In OS Terrain 50 GeoPackage naming, spotHeightType became spot_height_type.
In OS Terrain 50 GeoPackage naming, waterLevelCategory became water_level_category and contourLineType became contour_line_type.
The OS Terrain 50 known-data-issues page currently reports no live known data issues and retains resolved issue details only until the next product release.
